chunks: What SI/PI are and why they matter. The question: What is SI/PI? Why is it important?
Signal integrity (SI) asks whether a signal arrives at the receiver intact: the right voltage, at the right time, with a clean shape.
Power integrity (PI) asks whether a chip gets a steady supply voltage even when its demand for current suddenly jumps.
They are linked: a noisy supply spoils signals, and switching signals make supply noise.
Think of a house's water system. Sending a pulse down a pipe and getting a clean pulse out the other end is signal integrity.
Keeping the water pressure steady at one tap when a neighbor flushes a toilet is power integrity. A sudden flush makes pressure sag everywhere on that line.
Likewise, a chip's sudden current demand makes the supply voltage sag, and that sag can shift the moment the chip's outputs switch.
SI and PI are driven by the same trends and meet in the return path and the supply. Supply noise becomes jitter; switching current becomes ground bounce.
Signal integrity (SI): signals arriving with the right level, timing and shape. Power integrity (PI): the supply staying within its allowed voltage range.
Reflection: part of a signal bouncing back from an abrupt change in the wire ("Reflections and why they matter").
Crosstalk: a signal leaking into a neighboring wire ("Crosstalk").
Decoupling capacitor: a small energy store placed next to a chip that supplies sudden bursts of current ("Decoupling capacitors and when needed").
A chip runs from a 1 volts supply that may only wobble by 3%, which is 30 millivolts. Its demand suddenly jumps by 10 amps.
The supply path, capacitors included, behaves like a small resistance R (its impedance), and it drops 10 amps times R.
To stay within 30 millivolts, R must be at most 30 millivolts / 10 amps = 3 milliohms. No single capacitor is that good, so PI uses many decoupling capacitors.
SI covers the signals leaving that chip. If the supply sags, the chip's output edges shift in time, which shows up as timing error called jitter ("Jitter").
That is the whole idea: clean signals need a clean supply.
"Signal integrity is whether a signal arrives intact: reflections, ringing, crosstalk, loss, jitter and ground bounce.

Power integrity is whether the chips get a clean, stable supply: IR drop, ripple, and transient droop, handled by designing the power delivery network impedance below a target of allowed ripple over transient current.
They are linked, because supply noise becomes jitter and shared return paths couple signals.
They matter because voltages are low, edges are fast and currents are large, so margins are tens of millivolts and picoseconds."
